query: Consider the following context: The ability to endure extreme corrosion in challenging environments is reduced in stainless steel. This can be addressed by appropriate surface modification techniques to redefine the surface with the required properties. In that context, which method can be used for improved corrosion resistance, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A machine-learning workflow that integrates existing composition, processing, and corrosion data can be used to predict optimal deposition parameters for forming nanocrystalline high-entropy alloy (HEA) films on stainless steel, which will significantly improve its corrosion resistance in harsh environments.
generation.material_initial_state: Conventional stainless steel that relies on passive oxide layers which degrade under extreme corrosive conditions (e.g., high chloride or molten salt environments).
generation.intervention: Apply a surface modification process using deposition of an HEA film (e.g., a refractory high-entropy alloy film) whose composition and processing parameters are selected via a machine-learning model.
generation.conditions: Exposure to aggressive corrosive media such as high-temperature chloride-containing or molten salt environments where traditional passive films fail.
generation.structural_mediator: A nanocrystalline HEA film with a refined grain structure that forms a dense and adherent barrier layer on the stainless steel substrate.
generation.mechanism: The optimized HEA coating, designed via machine-learning insights, creates a self-healing, compact and protective layer that limits elemental leaching and impedes corrosive species, thereby preserving surface integrity under harsh conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: A measurable reduction in corrosion rate and improved surface durability compared to unmodified stainless steel, as indicated by lower weight loss, improved electrochemical performance, and enhanced mechanical properties such as increased hardness.
generation.baseline: Uncoated stainless steel or stainless steel coated using conventional trial-and-error methods that do not achieve as refined microstructure or adherence, leading to higher corrosion rates under the same conditions.
generation.boundary: The efficacy of the method may vary with specific environment types (e.g., molten salts vs. high-temperature chloride solutions) and might be limited if the ML predictions do not account for unforeseen factors affecting coating adhesion or stability at extremely high temperatures.
generation.uncertainty: Although initial evidence from HEA coating studies (e.g., improved corrosion resistance on stainless steel substrates) supports the potential of this approach, the precise magnitude of corrosion resistance improvement and the robustness of the machine-learning predictions across all harsh environments remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of stainless-steel samples: one set coated with an HEA film using parameters optimized by a machine-learning model and a control set coated using a standard, non-optimized process. Expose both sets to a harsh corrosive environment (e.g., 3.5 wt% NaCl solution at elevated temperature or molten salt environment) for a fixed time period.
measurements: Corrosion rate via weight loss measurements
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) and potentiodynamic polarization tests
Microstructural analysis using X-ray diffraction (XRD) and electron microscopy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the machine-learning optimized HEA coatings do not show a statistically significant improvement in corrosion resistance (i.e., similar or higher corrosion rates and inferior mechanical and microstructural properties) compared to the control coatings under identical test conditions, the hypothesis will be falsified.

The purpose of this work is to investigate the effect of the Cr content on the microstructure and properties of the WVTaTiCr x coating. The morphologies and phase compositions of five coatings with different Cr contents were comparatively observed. In addition, the hardness and high-temperature oxidation resistance of the coatings were also analyzed. As a result, with the increase in Cr, the coating grains were more refined. All the coating is mainly composed of the BCC solid-solution phase, which promotes the precipitation of the Laves phase with the increase in Cr. Development of high-entropy alloy (HEA) films is a promising and cost-effective way to incorporate these materials of superior properties in harsh environments. In this work, a refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) film of equimolar CuMoTaWV was deposited on silicon and 304 stainless-steel substrates using DC-magnetron sputtering. A sputtering target was developed by partial sintering of an equimolar powder mixture of Cu, Mo, Ta, W, and V using spark plasma sintering. The target was used to sputter a nanocrystalline RHEA film with a thickness of ∼900 nm and an average grain size of 18 nm. X-ray diffraction of the film revealed a body-centered cubic solid solution with preferred orientation in the (110) directional plane. The nanocrystalline nature of the RHEA film resulted in a hardness of 19 ± 2.3 GPa and an elastic modulus of 259 ± 19.2 GPa. A high compressive strength of 10 ± 0.8 GPa was obtained in nanopillar compression due to solid solution hardening and grain boundary strengthening. decision.trend: Earlier work compared stainless steels to newly developed high-entropy alloys in severe corrosion environments (e.g., FLiBe and molten chlorides). Studies revealed that standard stainless steels often lost protective performance under extreme conditions, but certain multicomponent coatings and films offered promise. In particular, depositing nanocrystalline or eutectic high-entropy alloy layers on steel substrates demonstrated improved mechanical or corrosion behavior. However, each study examined specific alloy families and process parameters in isolation, leaving a gap in systematically optimizing corrosion protection across a broader range of conditions.
decision.unsolved: It remains challenging to pinpoint the optimal surface modification or coating approach for stainless steels under diverse harsh environments without labor-intensive trial-and-error. The field lacks an overarching method to efficiently explore the large design space of coating compositions, processing routes, and application conditions in order to maximize corrosion resistance.
decision.lever: Use a machine-learning workflow integrating composition, processing, and corrosion data from existing alloy/coating studies to predict optimal surface modification parameters and accelerate the design of corrosion-resistant stainless steels.
decision.why: Machine learning can rapidly correlate process conditions, alloy or coating compositions, and key performance outcomes, enabling rational selection and fine-tuning of surface modifications. This approach builds on past experimental evidence and reduces trial-and-error, expediting the development of improved corrosion-resistant stainless-steel surfaces for harsh operating environments.
